cards.title: Launch order for an ecommerce Google Ads account
cards.summary: Sequence campaign types bottom-funnel first (Search/Shopping), then remarketing/PMax, then Demand Gen top-funnel last.
cards.use_when: Planning which campaign types to launch first for a new or restructured ecommerce Google Ads account.
steps: Start with Search and Shopping (bottom/mid funnel) so the account begins driving new customers and branded data immediately.

After the account has roughly 4–6 weeks of data (source's guideline, not strict — depends on budget, product, and sale volume; can be sooner at high spend), add step two: direct remarketing via video and display campaigns to users who visited, added to cart, or began checkout without purchasing.
Only introduce Demand Gen (step three) once bottom and mid-funnel are largely saturated, because top-of-funnel conversions cost more and bottom-funnel traffic converts cheaper and higher quality.
Exception the source allows: if you already run proven creatives on Meta and are a large account, you may port them into Demand Gen earlier for profitable cold acquisition.
For video cold traffic, use Demand Gen with video-only assets, since the older video campaign type is being sunset by Google (verify current interface).
caveats: The 4–6 week figure is a general guideline, explicitly variable by budget and sales volume.

cards.title: Separate branded vs non-branded campaigns
cards.summary: Never mix branded and non-branded targeting in one campaign — split for new-customer acquisition, clean attribution, and correct algorithm signals.
cards.use_when: Structuring new Search or Shopping campaigns, or diagnosing muddled attribution and inflated metrics in an ecommerce account.
steps: Define branded search as any query containing your brand name with inherent brand intent (e.g., 'Peter's Pans'); non-branded as generic product terms (e.g., 'non-stick fry pan').
Split every campaign into a branded stream and a non-branded stream rather than combining them.
Add your brand terms as exact-match negative keywords in every non-branded campaign so branded searches cannot leak in and distort attribution.
Expect your scaling to come from non-branded campaigns; branded campaigns exist mainly to capture existing demand cheaply and feed the algorithm data.
In the account, keep budget allocated so branded campaigns do not accidentally absorb spend meant for non-branded growth.
caveats: Source holds the opinion that branded campaigns are 'absolutely necessary' and high-performing accounts always have one; he concedes some accounts benefit less. Treat this as his view; nothing in Google Ads is black-and-white.

cards.title: Bid strategy progression: clicks first, then conversions
cards.summary: Start new accounts on Maximize Clicks to gather conversion data, then switch to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS after enough conversions.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing bid strategy on a new ecommerce Google Ads account or one with too few conversions for smart bidding.
steps: Launch with Maximize Clicks so Google can win cheap clicks while the account has no conversion history.

Keep click-focused bidding until you have accumulated conversions; the source cites roughly 15–30 conversions per month as the threshold to consider moving to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS, and mentions 10–15 conversions as an earlier consideration point.
Rationale: asking a conversion-based strategy to find conversions in an account that has never recorded one is like blindfolding an archer — Google does not know what to aim at.
Once conversions exist, switch the campaign to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS to let smart bidding optimize toward revenue.
Aggregate conversion volume across the account when judging readiness, since the threshold is about signal volume, not any single campaign.
caveats: The 10–15 and 15–30 conversion figures are source-specific heuristics, not a documented calculation; treat as rough guides.

cards.title: Use branded campaigns as cheap algorithm training data
cards.summary: Run low-budget branded Search/Shopping to supply Google cheap, high-quality conversion data that accelerates learning in non-branded campaigns.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to bid on your own brand terms in ecommerce Google Ads.
steps: Accept that branded bidders would have converted anyway, and value the campaign for data instead: branded conversions are the cheapest source of high-quality traffic and signal.
Let branded conversion data flow into the account so machine learning improves on more expensive new-customer non-branded efforts.
Cap spend realistically — for smaller brands the source suggests roughly $10–$20/day, larger brands up to about $50/day, rare to exceed $50/day in the US.
If you fully spend the daily budget, check search terms under insights and reports; if traffic matches your brand intent, raise the budget until captured.
Set customer acquisition (new-customer) targeting off in branded campaigns; returning existing customers are fine there.
caveats: Google will not spend your full branded budget if there is not enough branded search volume — a low delivery is normal for small brands.

cards.title: Turn off Search Partners and Display Network for Search campaigns
cards.summary: Uncheck search partners and the Google Display Network in Search campaign settings to protect conversion quality.
cards.use_when: Configuring settings for a new ecommerce Search campaign, before launch.
steps: Leave the Google Search Partners Network unchecked: it adds reach but typically brings lower-quality traffic, fewer conversions, and higher cost per conversion.
Leave the Google Display Network unchecked too: if you want display placements, create a separate Display campaign.
Note both boxes are checked by default, so actively untick them each time you build a Search campaign.
Only reconsider search partners if you have absolutely exhausted everything available on Google proper — the source calls this a very rare scenario.
caveats: This is the source's default practice; he allows exceptions for saturated accounts but treats them as unusual.

cards.title: Set location targeting to presence, not presence-or-interest
cards.summary: Use 'presence' location targeting so ads only serve people actually in the target country, not those merely interested in it.
cards.use_when: Configuring geographic targeting on any ecommerce Google Ads campaign, especially when selling only to specific countries.
steps: In campaign settings, enter the target location and narrow it as far as needed (country, state, city, postcode).
Open the location options dropdown and select 'presence' rather than 'presence or interest'.
Reason: presence-or-interest can serve ads to people outside your target country who are merely interested in it (e.g., someone abroad searching about it), wasting spend.
Optionally exclude regions you do not want to serve.
Combine with a language setting that matches your store, typically English unless you sell in other languages.
Leave audience segments off unless you have a specific demographic to target, and keep broad match keywords off for these campaigns.

cards.title: Ignore Google's AI keyword and asset generation
cards.summary: Skip Google's automated keyword/asset generation during campaign setup — Google optimizes for its own revenue, not yours, and does not know your brand.
cards.use_when: Building new Search campaigns and facing Google's prompted tools or recommendations.
steps: On the keyword and asset generation screen, do not use the suggested AI keywords or headlines.
Apply the same skepticism throughout setup to any automated creation or automated change suggestions.
Rationale: Google will try to make as much money as they can, not necessarily as much for you, and knows your brand and customers less well than you do.
Add your own keywords manually with the intended match types instead.
Same logic applies to ad copy: the source says Google will tell you not to pin headlines; he disagrees and says pin when it improves relevance.
caveats: This is the source's strong opinion; other practitioners do use automated suggestions. Treat as a default stance, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Step 2: add remarketing to re-engage non-converting visitors
cards.summary: Build direct remarketing campaigns (video and display) targeting site visitors who added to cart or began checkout but did not purchase.
cards.use_when: After initial Search/Shopping campaigns are running and you want to recover near-converting traffic in an ecommerce store.
steps: Build audience lists from site behavior: visited, added to cart, began checkout, and prior purchasers for repeat purchase.
Run video remarketing campaigns for these audiences; the source finds video most effective when creatives are high quality because they are more engaging.
Alternatively or additionally run display remarketing campaigns to re-approach non-purchasers and past buyers.
Add these campaigns only after roughly 4–6 weeks of account data (source's guideline, variable by budget and sales volume).
Expect these to lift both conversion rate and customer LTV by adding repeated touchpoints.
Keep the goal to push users over the edge toward purchase and to re-trigger past customers, not to retarget broadly.
caveats: The 4–6 week timing is a general guideline, not strict.

cards.title: Use Performance Max correctly, or use feed-only PMax as the safer retargeting option
cards.summary: Standard PMax can retarget everywhere and exchange feed data with Shopping, but if mishandled it swallows traffic and derails attribution; feed-only PMax is the safer retargeting machine.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add Performance Max to an ecommerce account for mid-funnel retargeting.
steps: Understand standard PMax: it serves across search, shopping, display, video and more, and if given a product feed similar to Shopping it exchanges data, enabling retargeting of Shopping audiences with PMax's broad placement reach (Gmail, YouTube, etc.).
If new to Google Ads, prefer standard remarketing campaigns and avoid PMax unless you know what you are doing.

Consider a feed-only PMax — a PMax stripped of text, image, and video assets, forcing the algorithm to rely solely on the Google Merchant Center shopping feed for product remarketing — as the safer shopping-focused option.
Use the same feed as your Shopping campaigns so the two campaigns exchange data and build a high-quality funnel with repeated touchpoints.
Do not point a feed-only campaign at placements you do not want; keep it feeding from the Merchant Center feed (verify current interface since PMax options change).
caveats: Source warns PMax done incorrectly will swallow all traffic, ruin attribution, and possibly derail the account — it is not recommended for beginners.

cards.title: Introduce Demand Gen last, for top-of-funnel cold traffic
cards.summary: Use Demand Gen (video-only or all-assets) for cold audiences only after bottom and mid-funnel campaigns are saturated.
cards.use_when: Deciding when and how to run cold top-of-funnel Google Ads for an ecommerce brand.
steps: Target people who may not know the product, the problem, or your brand — e.g., a kitchen-cookware ad asking 'Are you sick of food sticking to your pans?' then showing a high-quality creative.

Choose between video-only Demand Gen (YouTube ads via video assets, kept in the preferred/future-proof campaign type since old video campaigns are being sunset) and all-assets Demand Gen (serves across YouTube, display, search, and more).
Start with video-focused setups: the source notes all-assets campaigns typically yield lower efficiency on video.
Delay launch until bottom-of-funnel and mid-funnel campaigns are largely saturated, because top-of-funnel conversions cost more.
Run it as a standalone full-funnel layer independent of other channels once proven; if you already have proven Meta creatives and a large account, port them here earlier for profitable acquisition.
caveats: Efficiency/cost expectations are the source's guidance, not measured benchmarks; the video campaign sunset timing is forecast and should be verified.

cards.title: Link Shopify and Merchant Center, then Merchant Center to Google Ads
cards.summary: Three-way linking (Shopify → Google Merchant Center → Google Ads) is the prerequisite for any Shopping or feed-based campaign.
cards.use_when: Preparing an ecommerce store to run Shopping or feed-based Google Ads for the first time.
steps: In Shopify, go to Sales channels → Google and YouTube and link your Google account and Merchant Center to Shopify, then link products.
If you have no Merchant Center, create one (merchants.google.com) and connect it to Shopify via that tab; allow a couple of hours for the link and product import.
In Google Ads, go to Tools → Data manager → connected products and connect Google Merchant Center if not already shown.
Verify your imported products appear on the Merchant Center products page before building campaigns.
If you are not on Shopify, use an equivalent linking solution for your platform (source notes most stores are Shopify but other tools exist).
caveats: Interface paths are as described at the time of recording; Google changes navigation, so verify current menus.

cards.title: Feed product titles with informative keywords
cards.summary: Write Merchant Center product titles that include the full product name, key attributes, and brand so Google matches them to the right searches.
cards.use_when: Optimizing Merchant Center product data before running Shopping campaigns.
steps: Put the highly necessary product details first in the title, then attributes, then the brand name at the end.
Example structure: 'Black Non-Stick Frying Pan 38cm Diameter, Peter's Pans'.
Include keywords that reflect what shoppers actually search, so Google can target the product ad to the right queries.
Fill every available field (title, description, product type, category, price, sale price, GTIN, etc.) with high-quality information.
If you have a GTIN, include it; if not, do not worry and still complete the rest.
Do not agonize over perfection at this stage — get a correct, informative setup live first; deep optimization is a separate, longer effort.
caveats: Title keyword strategy must not include terms your product is not (see incorrect-attribute warning card).

cards.title: Product descriptions: use AI for keyword-rich copy, but never wrong attributes
cards.summary: Generate long Merchant Center descriptions with a tool like ChatGPT, but exclude any attribute the product does not actually have.
cards.use_when: Filling Merchant Center product description fields across a catalog without hand-writing every one.
steps: Use a detailed prompt, e.g., 'Write a 2,000-character product description for a black 38cm non-stick frying pan, including keywords a shopper might Google to trigger a Shopping ad.'
Treat the description as a keyword surface for Google's matching, not as marketing copy that must be hand-written.
Only include keywords for products and searches you actually want to appear for.
Exclude incorrect attributes: if a pan is not aluminum, do not write 'aluminum pan', or Google may serve it to aluminum or stainless steel pan searches and waste clicks.
Review generated descriptions before saving to catch any fabricated attributes.
Save your changes or the work is lost.
caveats: Wrong attribute terms cause Google to show the product to irrelevant searches, so cheap AI generation must still be checked.

cards.title: Use feed management tools for large catalogs
cards.summary: For large product catalogs, use a feed management app rather than editing every Merchant Center field manually.
cards.use_when: Working with a large SKU count and standard Shopify–Merchant Center sync is too slow or limited.
steps: Recognize that manually filling every field does not scale for large catalogs.
Use a Shopify feed management plugin (the source names Srois, a Shopify plugin) to manage feeds more thoroughly than the automatic Google–Shopify integration.
Apply it to bulk-edit titles, descriptions, and attributes across many products.
If you have only a few products, skip this and hand-fill the fields — simpler and faster.
After any bulk changes, verify in Merchant Center that products imported and are eligible to serve.
caveats: The source explicitly does not go deep into optimization and promises a future guide; treat this as a starting point. Tool names and plugins change — verify availability.

cards.title: Configure Shopping campaign objective and conversions
cards.summary: In Shopping campaign setup, select the sales objective and use only the purchase conversion goal — not add to cart or begin checkout.
cards.use_when: Creating a Shopping campaign for an ecommerce store and choosing conversion goals.
steps: In Campaigns, create a new campaign and choose the Sales objective (the source says this is the case ~99% of the time for ecommerce).
Set the account goal to purchases only; remove add to cart and begin checkout as conversion goals for this campaign.
Rationale: if Google can optimize to 'easy' micro-conversions, it may chase add-to-carts and never deliver purchases.
Ensure purchase conversion tracking is correctly installed before launch — bad tracking feeds poor data and undermines results.
Use a consistent campaign naming structure (campaign type → geography → focus, e.g., 'Shopping / USA / Non-Brand') so accounts are easy to review and audit.
caveats: Source treats purchases-only as the right default for ecommerce; it does not deny that add-to-cart and begin-checkout can be useful elsewhere in the account.

cards.title: Use Search for category/collection intent, Shopping for specific products
cards.summary: Route broad category searches to Search campaigns pointed at collection pages, and specific-product searches to Shopping listings.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a keyword should be covered by a Search campaign or left to Shopping listings in an ecommerce account.
steps: For non-branded Search, target category/collection intent (e.g., 'non-stick pans') where the shopper wants to compare a range rather than one exact product.
Send those clicks to the matching collection page (e.g., /nonstickpans), not a single product page.
Use phrase match for these category keywords; phrase match can get broad, so monitor and add negatives.
Keep ad groups to one collection/category each — never mix two collections in one ad group, or Google may show a crockpot searcher a non-stick pan ad.
Use Shopping for the 'sniper' approach — when someone searches a specific product spec, the exact product listing shows with image, price, and shipping.
Only run category Search campaigns when a category is genuinely popular and data supports testing it; they are not essential in most ecommerce accounts.
caveats: Source states Search campaigns are not a big priority in ecommerce and he uses them infrequently; Shopping is the main driver.

cards.title: Write branded vs non-branded Search ad copy
cards.summary: Include the brand name and pin it first in branded ads; emphasize range and guarantees in non-branded category ads.
cards.use_when: Writing RSA headlines and assets for branded or non-branded ecommerce Search campaigns.
steps: Branded ads: always include the brand name in a headline and pin it to position 1 so searchers instantly recognize your brand and click through.
Add a trust/social-proof headline (e.g., 'Ultimate Quality and Reliability') and an offer/CTA headline (e.g., a specific sale).
Non-branded category ads: the brand name is optional; instead lead with selection and reassurance, e.g., 'Huge Range of Non-Stick Pans' or a guarantee like '100% Guaranteed Not to Stick'.
For branded campaigns, set customer acquisition (new-customer) targeting off — returning customers are acceptable and desirable there.
Use only 3–5 headlines rather than filling all 15 so you can actually split test; too many headlines make testing impossible.
Pin headlines when it improves relevance, even though Google advises against pinning.
caveats: Source's anti-pinning position is a strong opinion that contradicts Google's recommendation; treat as a situational choice.

cards.title: Fill out ad extensions to expand ad real estate
cards.summary: Use sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets, promotions, prices, business name and logo to enlarge ads, build trust and lift CTR.
cards.use_when: Building Search ad assets for an ecommerce campaign and trying to maximize click-through rate.
steps: Add sitelinks to relevant but not immediately-matching pages (bestselling product, a why-non-stick blog post, etc.) so interested users can self-route.
Add callouts and structured snippets for trust and to build out the ad's footprint on the search page.
Test promotions and price assets; the source says they are useful but not strictly necessary.
Skip calls and messages — not relevant for ecommerce brands.
Complete advertiser verification to enable business name and logo on ads; source calls this worth the hassle because it raises trust, especially against competitors in non-branded auctions.
Write these once with care — they can be reused across nearly every campaign, so quality copy pays off long-term.
caveats: Bigger ads correlate with higher click chance per the source; asset types and availability change, so verify what your account supports.

cards.title: Set branded and category Search budgets
cards.summary: Keep branded budgets modest ($10–$50/day typical) and test category Search campaigns at roughly $20–$30/day based on AOV.
cards.use_when: Allocating daily budget to branded vs category Search campaigns for an ecommerce store.
steps: For branded campaigns, budget roughly $10–$20/day for smaller brands, up to about $50/day for larger brands; it is rare to exceed $50/day in the US.
Expect Google not to spend the full budget if branded search volume is low — a partial spend is normal.
For category Search campaigns, start around $20–$30/day to test, adjusting for AOV (higher AOV needs more budget to generate purchase volume) and total account budget.
If branded campaigns fully spend their budget, check search terms under insights and reports; if terms are aligned, increase budget until you capture the traffic.
Scale non-branded/category spend only when the data tells you it is warranted.
caveats: Figures are the source's rules of thumb, not benchmarks; actual spend depends on AOV, volume, and account size.

cards.title: Use negative keywords to protect non-branded campaigns
cards.summary: Add your brand terms as negatives in every non-branded campaign to stop branded searches leaking in and inflating metrics.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing non-branded Search or Shopping campaigns in an ecommerce account.
steps: Go to the ad group or campaign keywords area and open the negative keywords section.
Add every branded term you target in your branded campaign — brand name, misspellings, no-space variants — as negatives in the non-branded campaign.
Example: if a shopper searches 'Peter's Pans non-stick frying pan', without the negative they could land in the non-branded ad group and distort attribution.
Use a shared negative keyword list so the same brand terms can be applied across all non-branded campaigns.
Beyond brand terms, monitor phrase-match traffic and add negatives for irrelevant queries as they appear.
Re-check search terms regularly since broad phrase match drifts over time.

cards.title: Test category Search campaigns cautiously
cards.summary: Non-branded category Search campaigns are optional in ecommerce — only launch them when a popular category shows likely profitable demand.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to add non-branded category Search campaigns alongside Shopping.
steps: Default to letting Shopping carry non-branded product demand; only test category Search when one category gets heavy traffic and users likely to buy.
Keep ad groups tightly themed to a single category or collection.
Use 3–5 phrase-match keywords per category ad group, maximum 10 — three well-chosen phrases often capture the traffic.
Point ads to the matching collection page for a seamless journey from query to page.
Start at roughly $20–$30/day for the test and scale only if data supports a profitable ROI.
Drop or pause the campaign if data does not show profitable demand.
caveats: Source is candid that he does not use category Search campaigns frequently and considers them non-essential in most ecommerce accounts.
